deep.reconstruction:
Context: Riemann's fragment on linear differential equations with algebraic coefficients (1857, printed in the Werke Nachlass). A 'system' (y_1,...,y_n) is a vector of many-valued functions. Its only branch points are a,b,...,g. A positive circuit around a sends y to (A)y, with (A) a constant matrix, and similarly (B),...,(G) at the other branch points. Systems with the same substitutions form a 'class'. Near a, after a constant change of basis (beta), the system takes the form z_k ~ (x-a)^{mu_k}·(holomorphic, nonzero), possibly with logarithmic terms in degenerate cases.

Previous page. Take n+1 systems y^{(1)},...,y^{(n+1)} of one class. Consider the n x (n+1) matrix Y = (y_i^{(k)}). Seek a=(a_0,...,a_n) with Σ_k a_k y_i^{(k)} = 0 for i=1..n; these are the equations (2). By Cramer, a_k is proportional to ±D_k, where D_k is the n x n minor with column k deleted. Each D_k = Σ± y_1^{(1)}...y_n^{(n)} is multiplied by det(A) after a circuit around a. It has no essential singularity there, so it expands in integer-step powers of (x-a) times a fixed power. Writing D = det(beta)·Σ± z..., the lowest exponent is at least mu-bar = min over permutations of Σ_i mu_i^{(sigma(i))}. Define nu-bar, ..., rho-bar similarly at b, ..., g.

This page, step 1. F(x) = D·(x-a)^{-mu-bar}(x-b)^{-nu-bar}...(x-g)^{-rho-bar} has the following properties.
- It is single-valued, since exp(2πi·mu-bar) = det(A); this is implicit.
- It is finite at every finite x.
- At x=∞ it grows at most like x^{-(mu-bar+...+rho-bar)}. This is implicit: ∞ is not a branch point, so D is bounded there.

By Liouville/Riemann removable-singularity reasoning, F is therefore a polynomial of degree ≤ -(mu-bar+...+rho-bar). Hence, if D is not identically 0, -(Σ exponents) is a non-negative integer.

Step 2. Apply this to every minor D_k: D_k = P_k(x)·Π(x-a)^{mu-bar_k}... with P_k polynomial. For fixed a, all mu-bar_k are congruent mod Z, since every exp(2πi·mu-bar_k) equals det(A). So the ratios D_k/D_j are rational functions. Clearing the common factor, a_0,...,a_n can be taken to be polynomials. This is the theorem: between any n+1 systems of one class there is a linear homogeneous relation with polynomial coefficients.

Step 3. d/dx commutes with the constant matrix (A), so (y_1',...,y_n') is again a system of the same class.

Corollary 1. Apply the theorem to y, y', ..., y^{(n)}. This gives a_0 y + a_1 y' + ... + a_n y^{(n)} = 0 with polynomial a_k, an n-th order ODE with polynomial coefficients.

Corollary 2. Apply it to Y, y, y', ..., y^{(n-1)}. This gives c_0 Y = b_0 y + ... + b_{n-1} y^{(n-1)}, so every system of the class is a combination of y,...,y^{(n-1)} with rational coefficients. In modern terms the class is a vector space of dimension n over C(x), cyclically generated by y under d/dx.

Outlook. A general expression for all systems of a class follows, which shows there are infinitely many. Riemann announces it will be used to find all systems with the same substitutions and the same exponents; this is carried out on the next page.
errors: No real error. Implicit assumption: x=∞ is not a branch point (the y's are regular there), which is needed for D to be bounded at ∞ and for the stated degree bound. Branch points are a..g, all finite, so this is consistent.
The single-valuedness of D·Π(x-a)^{-mu-bar} uses det(A) = exp(2πi·mu-bar). This is stated only implicitly, and mu-bar is fixed only modulo the choice of exponents.
The 'lowest exponent ≥ mu-bar' argument tacitly ignores logarithmic terms for coinciding exponents. Logs only shift by bounded powers, so the conclusion survives.
Corollary 1 needs a_n ≠ 0, i.e. det(y_i^{(j)})_{j<n} ≢ 0. This holds when y_1..y_n are linearly independent over C. Likewise c_0 ≠ 0 in corollary 2. Both nondegeneracy conditions are unstated.
If all n x n minors vanish identically (rank < n), the Cramer argument degenerates. A relation still exists, via smaller minors, but this case is not treated.

results.what: Determinant of n systems of one class, divided by Π(x-a)^{mu-bar}, is a polynomial of degree ≤ -(Σ exponents); hence -(Σ exponents) is a non-negative integer when the determinant is nonzero
results.modern_name: Fuchs relation / Wronskian (Abel–Liouville) exponent-sum constraint for Fuchsian systems

results.what: Any n+1 systems with the same monodromy satisfy a linear relation with polynomial coefficients
results.modern_name: Monodromy class of rank n is an n-dimensional C(x)-vector space (regular-singular connection / D-module)

results.what: Given monodromy, the functions satisfy an n-th order ODE with polynomial coefficients; every system of the class is a C(x)-linear combination of y,...,y^{(n-1)}
results.modern_name: Riemann's approach to the Riemann–Hilbert problem; cyclic vector

results.what: Derivatives of a system have the same monodromy
results.modern_name: d/dx commutes with constant monodromy matrices

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's known 1857 fragment 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten', printed in the Gesammelte Werke Nachlass (1876). Its content is well known and credited to him, so the page only matters as manuscript confirmation of that text.

checkable.asserts: Determinant of systems (y,y') for y=(x^alpha,x^beta) equals const·x^(mu-bar), with mu-bar = alpha+(beta-1) the minimal exponent sum; result 0

checkable.asserts: Corollary 1 example: the minors of [y,y',y''] yield the polynomial-coefficient ODE x^2y''+(1-alpha-beta)xy'+alpha*beta*y=0; both entries 0

checkable.asserts: Each 2x2 minor equals a polynomial times x^(exponent), with exponents differing by integers, so the a_k are proportional to polynomials

transcription_corrections: 'einändrig' is most likely 'einwerthig' (single-valued); the published text reads 'einwerthig und endlich'.
The barred exponents mu-bar, nu-bar, rho-bar are the minima mu, nu, ... defined on the previous page.
'Corollare' is written as 'Corollare' with Riemann's quotation marks around both statements; the content matches the transcription.
